output.brief: The overtime overrun is mainly not a hiring-freeze problem. Call-back pay rose from $38k to $289k. Of 2,295 call-backs, 1,962 are closing work coded CLOSE, and all of them start on or after 1 April. That is when the $96k closing contract lapsed and the work moved to maintenance staff. Each short closing round is paid as a 3-hour minimum. The three districts that lost the contract show call-back increases of about $75–90k each. Summit Hill, which kept its contract, shows almost none. Regular holdover overtime is nearly flat, with hours up 1.5%. That argues against vacancies and heat as the main drivers. Vacancies do matter, since they raise fatigue and workload, but they don't explain the overrun. Eastgate has only 1 vacancy and still shows the same jump. Internal Audit checked the fraud allegation against lock logs and found no evidence of it. The Eastgate favoritism claim is unresolved. The supervisor's sign-up sheets were thrown away, and she says the same few people volunteer. The injury rise tracks overtime, but the claim records can't show a link to hours worked. My confidence is high on the closing-contract finding and moderate elsewhere. Next steps: restore or re-tender the closing contract, and track call-back spend. Review the 3-hour minimum with the union. Keep the sign-up sheets, and check how call-backs are shared. Don't impose an overtime cap or discipline anyone yet. Don't treat the freeze exemption as the fix.
